questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A fund has an expense ratio of 0.50%. How much does it cost per year on a $8,000 investment?
questions.intro: An expense ratio is the yearly cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percent of the money invested. It is taken out of the fund's assets automatically, so you never see a bill, but it lowers your return. Annual cost = amount invested × expense ratio.

misconceptions.C: Uses the percent as dollars per hundred

sources: SEC Investor.gov: Ongoing fees such as expense ratios reduce investment returns, and the effect compounds over time. (https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/understanding-fees)

questions.prompt: Two funds hold similar investments. Fund A charges 0.04%; Fund B charges 1.04%. On $20,000, how much more does Fund B cost per year?

sources: SEC Investor.gov: Ongoing fees such as expense ratios reduce investment returns, and the effect compounds over time. (https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/understanding-fees)

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: $10,000 grows for 30 years at 7% a year before fees. With a 0.05% fee, it grows to about $75,063; with a 0.75% fee, about $61,641. How much does the higher fee cost over 30 years?
questions.intro: Fees reduce returns every year, and the lost growth compounds. A difference that looks small each year can become large over decades.

misconceptions.A: Uses one year of the fee difference
misconceptions.B: Uses 30 years of simple fees on $10,000

They are taken from the fund automatically, not billed
